title: Jacket Potato with Prawn Marie Rose
subtitle: Baked potato with cold prawns in classic pink Marie Rose sauce
excerpt: Jacket potato with prawn Marie Rose is a British classic: a baked potato split and filled with cold cooked prawns in the creamy, slightly tangy Marie Rose sauce made from mayonnaise, ketchup, lemon, and a pinch of cayenne. It is a retro combination that has returned to British menus and remains deeply satisfying.
sourceNotes: Marie Rose sauce was popularised by Fanny Cradock in the 1960s as the dressing for prawn cocktail. The prawn and Marie Rose jacket potato became a staple of British pub and brasserie menus in the 1980s and remains part of the classic baked potato canon.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The Marie Rose sauce keeps in the fridge for 2 days.

content.text: Jacket potato with prawn Marie Rose comes together in minutes once the potato is baked. The Marie Rose sauce is a simple mix of mayonnaise, ketchup, lemon, and cayenne -- it should taste creamy, slightly sweet, and sharp. Cold prawns on a hot baked potato with a generous amount of sauce and some crunchy lettuce is a lunch combination that has earned its place in the British cooking canon.

Preheat the oven to 200C. Rub the {{potatoes-floury}} baking potatoes all over with {{olive-oil}} of olive oil and season generously with {{salt-table}} of salt. Pierce with a fork. Place directly on the oven rack and bake for 1 to 1.25 hours until completely cooked through and the skin is crisp.
Make the Marie Rose sauce and serve

Mix together {{mayonnaise}} of mayonnaise, {{ketchup}} of ketchup, the juice of {{lemon}} lemon, {{cayenne-pepper}} of cayenne, and {{worcestershire-sauce}} of Worcestershire sauce. Taste and adjust: it should be creamy, slightly tangy, and faintly spiced. Toss the {{prawns-cooked}} of cold cooked prawns in the sauce to coat.
Score a cross in each potato and squeeze the sides to open. Lay a little shredded {{lettuce}} iceberg lettuce inside, then pile the prawn Marie Rose on top. Serve with {{lemon}} lemon wedges.

items.cause: Too much ketchup or not enough lemon.
items.fix: Add more lemon juice and a little more Worcestershire sauce to balance. The sauce should not taste primarily of ketchup -- the mayonnaise should be the dominant element.

content.text: Marie Rose sauce is the dressing from the 1960s prawn cocktail, popularised by Fanny Cradock. The same sauce on a jacket potato rather than on lettuce became a standard pub and brasserie lunch in the 1980s. That was the same era that produced baked potato bars in shopping centres and high streets. The combination still has a loyal following and appears on menus as both nostalgia food and everyday lunch.
